title: Ecclesiastes
subtitle: Qohelet, “The one who gathers”
description: The Bible’s most honest book about the limits of life, spoken by the Teacher, a king in Jerusalem who tried wisdom, pleasure, great works and wealth, and found that “Everything is a breath.” The sun rises and sets, the wind goes round, the wise die like fools and the righteous sometimes perish, and no one can see the whole of what God is doing. Yet again and again the Teacher turns to say that bread and wine, work and love are gifts from the hand of God, to be received with joy. A time for everything under the heavens, a cord of three strands, bread sent out on the waters, “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth”, and the end of the matter: fear God and keep his commandments. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Ecclesiastes about?
qa.answer: Ecclesiastes is a search for what lasts. Its speaker, the Teacher, tests wisdom, pleasure, great works, wealth and long life to see what anyone gains from all their hard work “under the sun”, and finds that everything is hevel, a breath: brief, beyond grasping, and leaving no lasting profit. He faces injustice, loneliness and above all death, which comes to the wise and the foolish alike. Yet seven times he commends joy, the simple goods of food, work and love received as God’s gift, and the book ends: “Fear God and keep his commandments, because this is the whole of being human” (12:13).

qa.question: Who wrote Ecclesiastes?
qa.answer: The book calls its speaker Qohelet, “the one who gathers” an assembly, translated “the Preacher” in older Bibles and “the Teacher” here, and introduces him as “David’s son, king in Jerusalem” (1:1). It never gives his name. Jewish and Christian tradition long received the book as Solomon’s, and chapter 2 recalls his wisdom, building and wealth. Many scholars, noting that its Hebrew is among the latest in the Bible, think a later sage wrote it in Solomon’s person, perhaps in the fifth to third centuries BC. A second voice frames the Teacher’s words at the beginning and the end (1:1–2; 12:8–14).

qa.question: What does “vanity of vanities” mean?
qa.answer: It is the traditional English rendering of the book’s opening cry (1:2). The Hebrew word, hevel, used nearly forty times in Ecclesiastes, means a breath or a puff of vapour, the breath you see on a cold morning, real and then gone. It is also the name of Abel. The Teacher uses it of what is brief, of what cannot be grasped or understood, and of what comes to nothing. “Vanity” once meant emptiness but now suggests conceit, and “meaningless” keeps only one of its senses, so this translation keeps the picture: “Breath upon breath, says the Teacher, breath upon breath! Everything is a breath.” The doubled form is a Hebrew superlative, like “Song of Songs”.

qa.question: Is Ecclesiastes a pessimistic book?
qa.answer: Readers have long debated it. The Teacher speaks bluntly about injustice, the shortness of life and death, and sets sayings side by side that seem to pull against each other: sorrow is better than laughter (7:3), yet eat your bread with joy (9:7). Some read him as a man of faith clearing away false hopes so that only God and his gifts remain; some as an honest sceptic whose doubts the closing frame answers; some as a deliberate portrait of how life looks “under the sun”, set in Scripture to point the reader higher. What is clear is that God is present throughout the book, that joy is repeatedly commended as his gift, and that the book ends in the fear of God and the certainty of his judgment.

qa.question: What does “a time for everything” mean in Ecclesiastes 3?
qa.answer: Ecclesiastes 3:1–8 is a poem of fourteen pairs — a time to give birth and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to root up, a time to cry and a time to laugh, a time for war and a time for peace — which says that every matter under the heavens has its set time. It is both a comfort and a humbling: our times come to us, and we do not choose them. A few verses later the Teacher adds that God “has made everything fitting in its own time” and “put a sense of eternity in their hearts”, though no one can discover the whole of his work (3:11).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Its poems are set line by line, and the book’s keyword is rendered “breath” throughout. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
